column1: What was the last film you saw and your conclusion was "This is the worst acting I have ever seen"? The last film that had me cringing from start to finish was *Catwoman* (2004), starring Halle Berry. Now, Halle is undeniably a talented actress with an Oscar to her name, but this movie was an absolute trainwreck from an acting standpoint—hers included. The film seemed to exist in a vacuum where subtlety and nuance had been banished, leaving behind a parade of exaggerated facial expressions, stilted dialogue delivery, and bizarre choreography that felt more like a parody than a serious action flick. Berry’s performance was so over-the-top it was as if she’d been directed to channel the spirit of a cartoon cat rather than a complex, human character. The supporting cast wasn’t any better, with every line delivered with the emotional depth of a soap opera actor on their first day on set.   The script was a mess, of course, but even the worst material can be salvaged by a great actor. Unfortunately, no one in this film seemed to care enough to try. Every scene felt like a missed opportunity, from the awkward romance subplot to the climactic CGI-heavy fight sequences that looked more like a video game cutscene than a cinematic moment. What’s truly baffling is how a film with an A-list actress, a decent budget, and a popular comic book character as its source material could fail so spectacularly. It wasn’t just bad acting; it was a masterclass in how *not* to do it. By the time the credits rolled, I was left with one thought: “This must be what it’s like to watch a career implode in real-time.” And to think, Halle Berry won a Razzie for this role and actually showed up to accept it—an act of humility, maybe, but also a sad acknowledgment of just how far this film missed the mark.

What does a $1,500,000 house look like where you live? In Trinidad and Tobago, a $1,500,000 house is less about the structure itself and more about the statement it makes. It’s less of a home and more of a “look at me” proclamation, often perched on a hill or nestled in an exclusive gated community, complete with high walls, electric fences, and the obligatory security cameras. It’s the kind of house that screams, “I’ve made it,” even if the owner is drowning in debt to maintain the illusion.    Architecturally, it’s a mishmash of styles—part Mediterranean villa, part modern minimalist, with a touch of Caribbean flair thrown in for good measure. Think terracotta roofs, sprawling verandas, and infinity pools that seem to merge with the ocean or the lush green hills in the distance. Inside, it’s all open-plan living, high ceilings, and floor-to-ceiling windows that flood the space with natural light (and, inadvertently, the occasional tropical downpour).    The kitchen is a chef’s dream, complete with marble countertops, state-of-the-art appliances, and a massive island that somehow doubles as a gathering spot for family and friends. The master bedroom is a sanctuary, with a walk-in closet the size of a small apartment and an ensuite bathroom that feels more like a spa. And let’s not forget the “entertainment” spaces—the home theater, the wine cellar, and the outdoor barbeque area that’s perfect for hosting lavish weekend parties.    But here’s the catch: for all its grandeur, the house often feels more like a showpiece than a home. It’s the kind of place where you tiptoe around, afraid to leave fingerprints on the glass or scuff the polished floors. It’s where the air conditioning is cranked up so high you need a sweater in the Caribbean heat, and where the family spends more time in their individual “wings” than they do in shared spaces.    And yet, despite its impracticalities, it’s the dream—the ultimate symbol of success in a society that values appearances above all else. It’s the house that says, “I’ve arrived,” even if, deep down, the owner knows they’re still figuring out the destination.

Have you ever sabotaged food because someone was stealing it? Have you ever sabotaged food because someone was stealing it? Honestly, I’ve never gone full-on *vendetta mode* with someone’s lunch, but I’ve definitely entertained the thought more than once. There’s something so deeply personal about food theft—it’s not just about the meal, it’s about the time, effort, and sometimes even the emotional investment that went into preparing it. I remember this one time at work when I brought in a batch of homemade brownies. They were *perfect*—fudgy, rich, and with just the right amount of gooeyness in the center. I left them in the shared fridge, wrapped neatly in foil, and by lunchtime, they were gone. No note, no apology, just *poof*—vanished. Everyone denied it, of course, but I had my suspicions.    The next week, I made another batch. Same recipe, same perfection, but this time I added a secret ingredient: an unholy amount of salt. I wrapped them up just as neatly, left them in the fridge, and waited. Sure enough, by mid-morning, they were gone again. The look on my coworker’s face when she took that first bite was priceless. She didn’t say a word, just spat it out and glared at me like I’d committed a war crime. I casually shrugged and said, “Oh, I guess I must’ve messed up the recipe.” She never touched my food again.    But here’s the thing—I don’t feel bad about it. If anything, I feel like I taught her a valuable life lesson: don’t mess with someone’s brownies. Food theft is a violation of trust, and sometimes, a little sabotage is the only way to restore the balance. That said, I wouldn’t go as far as some people I’ve heard about—like the guy who added ghost pepper extract to his sandwich because he knew his coworker had a weak stomach. That’s just cruel. My approach is more about sending a message than causing actual harm. After all, it’s not about revenge—it’s about respect. And if a salty brownie is what it takes to get that point across, so be it.

What was your cringiest moment with a boss? My cringiest moment with a boss happened during a team meeting when my manager decided to share his thoughts on what he called “office culture.” He started by saying, “You know, I’ve always believed that a good office is like a family. And in every family, there’s a mom and a dad.” He then proceeded to point at himself and say, “I’m the dad, obviously.” Half of the room chuckled awkwardly, while the other half just stared at him in disbelief. But he wasn’t done yet. He pointed at our admin assistant, a woman in her late 50s, and said, “And *you* are the mom. You keep this family together.” She froze, clearly uncomfortable, and muttered something like, “Uh, sure,” before quickly looking down at her notes. The worst part? He didn’t even realize how inappropriate it was. He just moved on to the next agenda item as if he hadn’t just reduced her role to a cliché. I sat there, internally screaming, wondering how anyone thought this was a good idea. To make matters worse, later that day, he sent out a follow-up email titled “Our Office Family,” with a cartoon of a happy family holding hands. Everyone in the office spent the rest of the week avoiding eye contact with him and each other. It was one of those moments where you just wished the floor would open up and swallow you whole.    Another time, this same boss tried to bond with the team by sharing his favorite “joke,” which turned out to be a thinly veiled jab at one of our coworkers. The punchline was something like, “Well, at least *someone* here knows how to waste time!” Everyone laughed nervously, but it was painfully obvious who he was referring to. The coworker in question, who was sitting right there, forced a smile and excused himself from the room shortly after. My boss, seemingly oblivious, just kept going, “What? It’s funny, right? Lighten up, people!” Those moments made me realize that sometimes, no matter how much you respect someone’s position, there’s just no fixing a lack of self-awareness. It’s like watching a train wreck in slow motion—you know it’s going to be bad, but you can’t look away.

Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? It’s a question that lingers in the back of my mind more often than I’d like to admit. Life, as it turns out, is a series of hypotheticals and what-ifs, each one carrying its own weight of regret or relief. For some, the absence of children leaves a void, a quiet house that echoes with the laughter they’ll never hear. For others, the chaos of parenting feels like a constant reminder of freedoms sacrificed, dreams deferred, and a life irrevocably altered.  I’ve watched friends and family navigate these waters—some with grace, others with a palpable sense of loss. One friend, a fiercely independent woman in her late 30s, once confessed to me that she mourns the child she never had. Not because she felt societal pressure, but because she could suddenly envision a version of her life where she was a mother, and it was strangely beautiful. Another, a father of three, laughed bitterly one evening after his kids had finally gone to bed, muttering, “I love them more than anything, but sometimes I wonder who I’d be if I hadn’t had them so young.”  It’s a paradox, really. The things we don’t do haunt us just as much as the things we do. Regret, in this case, isn’t a failure or a weakness—it’s a testament to the complexity of human emotion. We’re wired to wonder, to second-guess, to imagine alternate realities where we might have been happier, more fulfilled, or simply different. And yet, there’s no universal answer. For every person who regrets not having kids, there’s another who wishes they’d waited—or never had them at all.  What’s fascinating, though, is how society frames this issue. We’re often made to feel that either choice is irrevocably wrong. But life isn’t binary. It’s messy, unpredictable, and full of gray areas. Perhaps the real question isn’t whether we regret having or not having kids—it’s whether we can make peace with the path we’ve chosen, knowing full well that the other road might have been just as bumpy, just as beautiful, and just as filled with regret.
